name: Epicureanism
era: From 306 BCE to the 3rd century CE, and revived since
line: Want little, fear nothing and keep your friends close.

quote.source: Principal Doctrines 2, in Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 10.139, trans. R. D. Hicks

quotes.text: Of all the means which are procured by wisdom to ensure happiness throughout the whole of life, by far the most important is the acquisition of friends.
quotes.source: Principal Doctrines 27, in Diogenes Laertius 10.148, trans. R. D. Hicks

quotes.text: It is impossible to live a pleasant life without living wisely and well and justly, and it is impossible to live wisely and well and justly without living pleasantly.
quotes.source: Principal Doctrines 5, in Diogenes Laertius 10.140, trans. R. D. Hicks

quotes.text: Let no one be slow to seek wisdom when he is young nor weary in the search thereof when he is grown old.
quotes.source: Letter to Menoeceus, in Diogenes Laertius 10.122, trans. R. D. Hicks

quotes.text: Send me a little pot of cheese, that, when I like, I may fare sumptuously.
quotes.source: From a letter, quoted in Diogenes Laertius 10.11, trans. R. D. Hicks

quotes.text: Nothing is sufficient for him to whom what is sufficient seems little.

words.usage: The house and garden outside Athens where Epicurus and his friends lived. The school took its name from it.
The goal of life. Epicurus means chiefly the absence of pain in the body and of trouble in the mind.
A mind without fear or anxious desire. The highest mental pleasure.
Not hungry, not thirsty, not cold. Once you have this, bodily pleasure can be varied but not increased.
The image Epicurus uses for a settled mind: water with no wind on it.
The storm in the soul that comes from fear and empty desire. The opposite of ataraxia.
The greatest means to a happy life. It begins from mutual help and becomes loved for itself.
The sober reckoning of what each choice will bring in pleasure and pain. Epicurus rates it above philosophy itself.
Being content with little, so that plenty is a bonus and scarcity no disaster.
The teaching in four lines: do not fear god, do not worry about death, what is good is easy to get, what is terrible is easy to endure.
The smallest bodies, solid and eternal, from which everything is made.
Empty space, in which atoms move. Atoms and void are all there is.
A tiny unpredictable shift in the path of an atom. Lucretius calls it the clinamen. It lets worlds form and leaves room for free will.
Understanding how the world works, undertaken to cure fear of the gods and of death.
The Epicurean theory of knowledge: the tests by which we tell true from false.
The first test of truth. The senses do not lie. Error comes in with the opinions we add.
The general notion of a thing built up from many experiences, which lets us recognise the next one.
Pleasure and pain. They are nature’s own signals of what to choose and what to avoid.
False belief about what one needs. The source of desires that can never be filled.
Forty short sayings that members of the school learned by heart.
The advice to stay out of politics and the pursuit of fame.
Honest criticism between friends, given kindly. The Epicurean Philodemus wrote a handbook on it.
The monthly feast of the school, held on the twentieth day in memory of Epicurus and Metrodorus.
The state of the gods, who are untroubled and trouble no one. The wise person lives like a god among mortals.
The Epicurean sage, who will be happy even on the rack, will marry only in some circumstances and will not make fine speeches.
Thinking a choice through by comparing its pleasures and pains over the long run.
Where the gods live, far from us and without concern for us.
Thunder, eclipses, comets. Epicurus offers several natural explanations for each, since any of them removes the fear.
The word Lucretius uses. His poem opens by calling Venus the pleasure of gods and men.
Lucretius’s name for the atomic deviation, in the second book of On the Nature of Things.

practices.name: The fourfold remedy
practices.instructions: Say the four lines aloud slowly, and after each one stop and test it against whatever is on your mind this morning. Nothing to fear from the gods. Nothing to feel in death. What is good is easy to get. What is terrible is easy to bear. If one line does not ring true today, say which and why. Then go on with the day.
practices.why: The tetrapharmakos, the four-part cure, is a summary of Epicurus’s ethics preserved by a follower in Herculaneum. It is short enough to say every morning.
variations: Write the four lines on a card.
Say them with a friend.
Pick the line you need most today.

practices.name: Sort your desires
practices.instructions: Write down everything you want today, large and small. Put each in one of three columns. Natural and necessary: food, water, warmth, safety, friends, a clear mind. Natural but not necessary: the tastier meal, the nicer room. Neither natural nor necessary: fame, luxury, more of everything. Cross out the third column and see how the day looks. The rule of this Onda is to want what is easy to get.
practices.why: Epicurus sorted desires into three kinds so that you could keep the cheap ones and drop the ones that make you anxious. The sorting itself brings calm.
variations: Sort your last purchases.
Sort the wants of a friend.
Do it at the end of the week.

practices.name: Tend a garden
practices.instructions: Spend fifteen minutes in a garden, real or tiny: a pot of herbs, a balcony box, a plot or a window shelf. Water, weed, pick, smell. Epicurus’s school was called the Garden, and it met in one. Sit for a moment among the plants and notice how little you need. Take one leaf with you.
practices.why: The Garden was both a place and a school: friends living simply among vegetables and fig trees. Even a pot of herbs is a small Garden.
variations: Grow something you can eat.
Sit by a plant for five minutes.
Visit a public garden.

practices.name: A doctrine for the day
practices.instructions: Choose one of the Principal Doctrines of Epicurus, short sayings of one or two sentences, and learn it by heart. Say it a few times on your way to work. Try Doctrine 1, on the blessed and the immortal, or Doctrine 3, on the limit of pleasure being the removal of all pain. Test it against your day.
practices.why: Epicureans memorised the doctrines so that they could recall them in a crisis. The Principal Doctrines are forty short sayings, easy to carry around.
variations: Write it on your hand.
Learn one a week.
Say it aloud to a friend.

practices.name: A glass of water, thirstily
practices.instructions: Drink a glass of water when you are properly thirsty, and notice how good it is. Epicurus said that water and barley bread give the highest pleasure to someone who needs them. Slow down and let the pleasure fill you. Notice that this pleasure was free and easy to get.
practices.why: Natural pleasures that meet real needs are the most reliable, in Epicurus’s view. A thirsty glass of water shows that.
variations: Eat a piece of bread when hungry.
Warm your hands on a cup.
Notice the pleasure of a stretch.

practices.name: Message a friend
practices.instructions: Write a warm message to a friend and send it. Say something real: that you are thinking of them, that you are grateful for them, that you would like to see them. Epicurus said that of all the things wisdom provides for a happy life, the greatest is the possession of friends. Use the morning to tend one.
practices.why: Friendship was central to the Garden. The doctrine is that friends bring more security and joy than anything money can buy.
variations: Call instead of writing.
Message someone you have not spoken to for months.
Make a plan to meet.

practices.name: Bread, water and a friend
practices.instructions: Make the simplest meal you can enjoy: good bread, water, perhaps olives, a piece of cheese or a bowl of lentils. Do not eat it alone. Sit with a friend, outside if possible, with no phones on the table. Eat slowly enough to taste it. Notice that you are as content as at a feast. The rule of this Onda is not to eat alone.
practices.why: Epicurus wrote that before you eat, you should consider with whom you eat, not what, because a meal without a friend is the life of a lion or a wolf.
variations: Share the meal on a bench.
Eat in silence for the first five minutes.
Invite someone who would eat alone.

practices.name: Study nature
practices.instructions: Pick one thing in the natural world that you do not understand or that vaguely frightens you: lightning, an illness, the size of the universe, what happens to a body after death. Spend twenty minutes learning how it actually works. Epicurus held that most fear comes from ignorance of nature. Write one calming fact.
practices.why: Physiologia, the study of nature, was an Epicurean tool for peace of mind. Once you know how thunder works, it stops being a threat.
variations: Look up how an eclipse happens.
Read about how the body ages.
Learn what a star is made of.

practices.name: Stay out of the race
practices.instructions: Choose one competition you are in today, for status, a promotion or a like, and step out of it deliberately. Do not compare, do not check, do not compete. Epicurus advised living unnoticed, lathe biosas, and staying out of public life if it troubles the mind. Notice the lightness. The rule of this Onda is to stay out of the race.
practices.why: Epicurus believed that ambition and the pursuit of fame disturb the mind. Opting out of one small race gives a taste of that peace.
variations: Skip checking the news for a day.
Decline an invitation to compete.
Let someone else win.

practices.name: Do a good deed unnoticed
practices.instructions: Do a favour for someone today in such a way that no one knows. Leave coffee money on the counter, mend a neighbour’s gate, send an anonymous note. Epicurus admired generosity, and living unnoticed. The pleasure of an unseen kindness is a quiet, lasting one.
practices.why: Lathe biosas, live unnoticed, is one of Epicurus’s best known sayings. A secret kindness makes the point well.
variations: Do it for a stranger.
Do it for someone you dislike.
Never tell anyone.

practices.name: Watch the dust
practices.instructions: Sit where a sunbeam falls into a room, and watch the dust motes drift. Lucretius, the Roman poet who retold Epicurus’s physics, describes dust in a sunbeam as an image of atoms moving in the void. Watch the randomness and the pattern for ten minutes. Notice that there is nothing here to fear.
practices.why: Lucretius uses the dancing dust in a sunbeam as his first picture of the atoms. Watching it brings the ancient physics to life.
variations: Watch rain on a window.
Watch leaves in the wind.
Watch clouds forming.

practices.name: An hour with a friend, no agenda
practices.instructions: Spend an hour with a friend with no plan: no tasks, no talking points, no phones. Walk, sit, cook something plain. Let the conversation wander. Friends in the Garden lived together and gave each other security and joy. Notice how little is needed for a happy hour.
practices.why: Epicurus taught that friendship is the greatest means to a blessed life. An hour with no agenda is its purest form.
variations: Do it outdoors.
Do it by phone with a far friend.
Do it with a family member.

practices.name: Remember past pleasures
practices.instructions: Before sleep, bring back three good things. One from today, one from this year, one from long ago. Take each slowly: who was there, what was said, how it felt in the body. Let the pleasure come again. Then give thanks for it. The rule of this Onda is to be grateful for what has been. Epicurus, dying in pain, said that the memory of his friends’ talks made him glad.
practices.why: Epicurus wrote on his last day that he was happy through the memory of past conversations. Recalling pleasures is a way to enjoy them twice.
variations: Write the three in a notebook.
Tell someone one of them.
Look at an old photograph.

practices.name: Read Lucretius aloud
practices.instructions: Read a passage of Lucretius’s On the Nature of Things aloud: the opening hymn to Venus, the sunbeam, or the closing lines of Book 3 on death. Choose a translation that sounds good, such as Stallings’s verse version. Read slowly, with feeling. The poem was meant to be heard, and is both beautiful and calming.
practices.why: On the Nature of Things is the finest poem of Epicurean philosophy, written by Lucretius around 55 BCE. Reading aloud makes its calm contagious.
variations: Read the opening to someone.
Listen to a recording.
Learn two lines by heart.

practices.name: A letter to a friend
practices.instructions: Write a proper letter to a friend, in the manner of Epicurus, who wrote to his friends constantly. Tell them what you have been thinking, what is cheering you, what you have learned. Say that you are well. Send it by post, if possible. Letters were how the Garden stayed together across the sea.
practices.why: Epicurus’s surviving letters to friends such as Menoeceus are among the best-loved philosophical texts. A letter is the Epicurean act of friendship.
variations: Write a letter on paper.
Include a pressed leaf.
Ask a question they must answer.

practices.name: Before you were born
practices.instructions: Sit quietly and think about the time before you were born. Was it painful? Did you suffer? Lucretius asks us to look at that long past with calm, and says that is the mirror of the time after death. Hold the thought for a few minutes. If it feels troubling, stop and think of something pleasant. Many people find this a relief.
practices.why: The symmetry argument says that nonexistence after death is no worse than nonexistence before birth. Many readers find it a surprising comfort.
variations: Read the passage in Lucretius first.
Do it in the garden at dusk.
Talk about it with a friend.

practices.name: A news-free evening
practices.instructions: Spend the evening without news, social media or anything that stirs anxiety. Epicureans sought ataraxia, freedom from disturbance. Cook something plain, talk, read, tidy a shelf. Notice what you do not miss. Go to bed with a quiet mind. The rule of this Onda is that serenity is the aim.
practices.why: Ataraxia, untroubled calm, is the goal of Epicurean life. A news-free evening is a modest and effective step toward it.
variations: Do it for a whole weekend.
Switch off notifications.
Read a book you love.

practices.name: Sit in the garden at dusk
practices.instructions: Go to a garden, park or balcony at dusk and sit among plants. Do nothing. Enjoy the cool air, the smell of leaves and the stillness. If a friend is with you, talk quietly or not at all. Epicurus’s school took its name from the Garden. Sit for fifteen minutes, and leave when the first star appears.
practices.why: The Garden was a place of peace. A quarter-hour among plants at the end of the day is a simple pleasure of the kind Epicurus recommended.
variations: Bring a cup of herbal tea.
Listen for evening birdsong.
Count the plants you can name.

practices.name: The Twentieth
practices.instructions: Hold a feast of the Twentieth with friends. Epicureans met on the twentieth of every month to eat together, remember Epicurus and share a simple supper. Serve bread, olives, cheese, lentils, figs and watered grape juice. Read a doctrine aloud, share what you are grateful for and tell a story. Keep it plain and happy.
practices.why: The Twentieth, Eikas, was the monthly feast of the Epicurean school. It was a regular occasion for friendship, memory and plain food.
variations: Keep it monthly.
Ask each guest to bring a doctrine.
End with a toast to absent friends.

practices.name: Make a pot garden
practices.instructions: Build a tiny garden in pots: herbs such as thyme, mint and parsley, or lettuces and tomatoes. Fill the pots with soil, sow or plant, water and label. Put them where they get light. Epicurus’s Garden grew the food of simple living. Eat from yours when it is ready, and share a leaf with a friend.
practices.why: Growing your own food is a small way to want what is easy to get. A pot garden costs little and returns much.
variations: Plant a window box.
Start from seed.
Give a pot to a friend.

immersePlan.name: Read the Letter to Menoeceus
immersePlan.text: Read Epicurus’s short letter on how to live happily. It is only a few pages. Underline the line about death.

immersePlan.name: Read a book of Lucretius
immersePlan.text: Read the opening hymn or the passage on the sunbeam from Lucretius’s great poem in A. E. Stallings’s translation. Read it aloud.

immersePlan.name: Read Travels with Epicurus
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Daniel Klein’s book about a man in his seventies who goes to a Greek island to see what the old philosopher meant by simple pleasures.

immersePlan.name: Watch Babette’s Feast
immersePlan.text: Watch Gabriel Axel’s film in which a cook spends everything on one glorious dinner for a severe Danish village. Notice how it changes them.

immersePlan.name: Watch Perfect Days
immersePlan.text: Watch Wim Wenders’s 2023 film about a Tokyo toilet cleaner who lives a plain, contented life of small pleasures. Notice what he notices.

immersePlan.name: Watch Alain de Botton on Epicurus
immersePlan.text: Watch the episode from The Consolations of Philosophy in which Alain de Botton explains Epicurus’s three keys to happiness: friends, freedom and thought.

immersePlan.name: Listen to the Seikilos epitaph
immersePlan.text: Play the oldest complete musical composition we have, a short tomb song that says while you live, shine. Hum along.

immersePlan.name: Listen to In Our Time on Epicureanism
immersePlan.text: Play the BBC discussion of Epicurus and his followers by three scholars. Listen while you walk.

immersePlan.name: Hear De Rerum Natura in Latin
immersePlan.text: Play a reading of the opening lines of Lucretius’s poem in Latin. Listen to the rhythm of the hexameters.

immersePlan.name: Look at the portrait head of Epicurus
immersePlan.text: Look at the Roman copies of a Greek portrait of Epicurus, with a calm brow and a thoughtful beard. Describe what you see.

immersePlan.name: Look at the skeleton cups
immersePlan.text: Look at the Roman silver cups engraved with skeletons and philosophers, reminding drinkers to enjoy life. Read the inscriptions.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Villa of the Papyri bronzes
immersePlan.text: Look at the statues found in the villa at Herculaneum, which held a library of Epicurean papyri. Pick one and imagine the owner.

immersePlan.name: Bake or eat barley bread
immersePlan.text: Bake or buy a loaf of barley bread and eat it with water. Notice how much pleasure a plain thing can give when you are hungry.

immersePlan.name: Eat a little pot of cheese
immersePlan.text: Eat a small piece of sheep or goat cheese with bread and olives. Epicurus asked a friend for a little pot of cheese so that he could feast when he liked.

immersePlan.name: Cook lentils and beans
immersePlan.text: Boil lentils or beans with a bay leaf, add oil and salt, and eat with bread. Share a bowl with a friend.

immersePlan.name: Drink spring water
immersePlan.text: Drink a glass of cold, clear water slowly, and notice its taste. It is the cheapest and most natural pleasure.

immersePlan.name: Drink thin grape juice
immersePlan.text: Mix grape juice with plenty of water and sip it. Epicureans favoured a little thin wine; juice keeps the lightness without the alcohol.

immersePlan.name: Raise a cup at the Twentieth
immersePlan.text: Pour a cup of watered grape juice at a shared supper and raise it to Epicurus and to your friends.

immersePlan.name: Hold a feast of the Twentieth
immersePlan.text: Share a plain supper with friends on the twentieth of the month, as Epicureans did, and read a doctrine aloud.

immersePlan.name: Learn about the open Garden
immersePlan.text: Read how the Garden admitted women and slaves as members, which was rare in Athens. Think about who you could invite to your table.

immersePlan.name: Learn a doctrine by heart
immersePlan.text: Choose one of the Principal Doctrines and learn it by heart, as Epicureans did. Repeat it three times today.

immersePlan.name: Play pente grammai
immersePlan.text: Play the Greek game of five lines, with five pieces each. Draw a board with five lines and use pebbles. Play two games.

immersePlan.name: Play knucklebones
immersePlan.text: Toss five small stones or dice in the air and catch them on the back of the hand. Play with a friend.

immersePlan.name: Play ball in the garden
immersePlan.text: Play a gentle game of catch in a garden or park with a friend or child. Exercise was a Greek pleasure.

immersePlan.name: Mark the Twentieth of the month
immersePlan.text: On the twentieth, share a plain meal with a friend and talk about something you are grateful for.

immersePlan.name: Keep Epicurus’s birthday
immersePlan.text: Epicurus’s birthday was kept every year by his followers with a feast. Raise a cup of water to him and read one saying.

immersePlan.name: Look up Herculaneum
immersePlan.text: Look at the buried town near Naples and the villa where charred scrolls of Epicurean philosophy were found. Read about how they are being read.

immersePlan.name: Practise ataraxia
immersePlan.text: Ataraxia is freedom from disturbance. Find one thing that disturbs you and take one step to remove it.

immersePlan.name: Practise lathe biosas
immersePlan.text: Lathe biosas means live unnoticed. Do one good thing today without telling anyone.

immersePlan.name: Practise philia
immersePlan.text: Philia is friendship. Spend ten minutes today giving a friend your full attention.

rules.text: Want what is easy to get
rules.why: Meet your natural needs and let go of desires that have no limit.
Find the company first and the food second.
Avoid the pursuit of fame, office and wealth. They cost more peace than they buy.
Ask what it will cost later. Refuse the pleasure that brings more pain, and accept the pain that brings more pleasure.
Where death is, you are not. Nothing in nature is out to punish you.

rules.text: Be grateful for what has been
rules.why: A good thing that has happened is yours for ever. Remember it.

read.title: Letter to Menoeceus
read.creator: Epicurus
read.why: His whole ethics in a few pages: the gods, death, desire, pleasure and prudence. Preserved by Diogenes Laertius.

read.title: Principal Doctrines
read.creator: Epicurus
read.why: Forty sayings for memorising. The first four are the fourfold remedy.

read.title: On the Nature of Things
read.creator: Lucretius, trans. A. E. Stallings or Martin Ferguson Smith
read.why: A Roman poet sets Epicurean physics to verse to free his reader from the fear of death. One of the great poems in Latin.

read.title: The Swerve: How the World Became Modern
read.creator: Stephen Greenblatt
read.why: The finding of the last copy of Lucretius in a German monastery in 1417, told as a detective story.

read.title: Travels with Epicurus
read.creator: Daniel Klein
read.why: A man in his seventies takes a suitcase of philosophy books to a Greek island to work out how to grow old.

read.title: How to Be an Epicurean
read.creator: Catherine Wilson
read.why: A historian of philosophy argues that this is the ancient school best suited to modern life.

watch.title: Epicurus on Happiness
watch.creator: Alain de Botton, in Philosophy: A Guide to Happiness
watch.why: A short television film on friends, freedom and thought as the three things Epicurus said we need.

watch.title: Babette’s Feast
watch.creator: Gabriel Axel
watch.why: A cook spends all she has on one dinner for a stern village. A film about what a shared table can do.

watch.title: Perfect Days
watch.creator: Wim Wenders
watch.why: A Tokyo toilet cleaner lives on little and enjoys trees, cassettes and paperbacks. Ataraxia without the word.

listen.title: The Seikilos epitaph
listen.creator: Seikilos; many recordings
listen.why: The oldest complete piece of music, carved on a tombstone in Asia Minor. Its words say to shine while you live, since life is short.

listen.title: Epicureanism
listen.creator: In Our Time, BBC Radio 4
listen.why: Three scholars on the Garden, the atoms and the reputation.

listen.title: History of Philosophy Without Any Gaps, episodes 55 to 59
listen.creator: Peter Adamson
listen.why: Five short, clear episodes on Epicurus and Lucretius.

listen.title: De Rerum Natura read in Latin
listen.creator: Many readers; recordings from the Society for the Oral Reading of Greek and Latin Literature
listen.why: Hear how the hexameters move, even without the language.

art.title: Portrait head of Epicurus
art.creator: Roman copies of a Greek original of about 270 BCE
art.why: A long, lined, serious face. Copies are in the Metropolitan Museum, the British Museum and the Capitoline. Followers kept his image on rings and cups.

art.title: The Boscoreale skeleton cups
art.creator: Roman silversmiths
art.why: Two silver cups in the Louvre on which skeletons labelled Epicurus and Zeno debate. An inscription beside Epicurus reads: pleasure is the goal.

art.title: The bronzes of the Villa of the Papyri
art.creator: From Herculaneum
art.why: Runners, dancers and busts of philosophers from the villa whose library was Epicurean. In the National Archaeological Museum, Naples.

art.title: The inscription of Diogenes of Oenoanda
art.creator: Oenoanda, Lycia
art.why: An old man had Epicurean teaching carved on a public wall some eighty metres long, as a gift to passers-by. Fragments are still being found.

eat.title: Barley bread
eat.creator: With water
eat.why: His daily food. He said bread and water give the highest pleasure when brought to someone hungry.

eat.title: A little pot of cheese
eat.creator: Sheep or goat cheese kept in brine
eat.why: What he asked a friend to send, so that he could feast when he liked.

eat.title: Lentils and beans
eat.creator: Boiled, with oil and salt
eat.why: During a siege of Athens he is said to have kept the school alive by counting out beans to each member.

eat.title: Figs, olives and garden greens
eat.creator: Whatever the plot gives
eat.why: The Garden grew its own vegetables. The school was probably the first in Athens to do so inside the city.

drink.title: Water
drink.creator: From the spring
drink.why: The usual drink of the Garden. Thirst met with water is a complete pleasure.

drink.title: Half a pint of thin wine
drink.creator: Well watered
drink.why: Diogenes Laertius says the friends were content with this much, and otherwise drank water.

drink.title: Wine at the Twentieth
drink.creator: Shared at the monthly feast
drink.why: The feast day was the one occasion for something better than the daily fare.

customs.title: The feast of the Twentieth
customs.creator: Monthly
customs.why: On the twentieth of each month the school dined together in memory of the founder and his friend Metrodorus, as his will directed.

customs.title: A school open to all
customs.creator: Women and slaves as members
customs.why: The Garden admitted women such as Leontion and Themista and slaves such as Mys. This was unheard of, and was used against it.

customs.title: Learning the doctrines by heart
customs.creator: Summaries and sayings
customs.why: Epicurus wrote short digests of his teaching so that students could carry it with them.

customs.title: Portraits of the master
customs.creator: Rings, cups and busts
customs.why: Epicureans kept his likeness about them and asked themselves how he would see what they were doing.

games.title: Pente grammai
games.creator: Board game · Greece
games.why: Five Lines. Two players race pieces along five lines by the throw of dice. The middle line was called the sacred line.

games.title: Knucklebones
games.creator: Game of skill and chance · Greece
games.why: Five sheep bones tossed and caught on the back of the hand. A game for a garden bench and two friends.

games.title: Ball play
games.creator: Exercise · Greece and Rome
games.why: Catching games played in a circle were thought the best gentle exercise. A Roman doctor wrote a whole essay in praise of the small ball.

festivals.title: Eikas, the Twentieth
festivals.creator: The 20th day of every month
festivals.why: A shared meal with friends, reading and talk. Modern Epicurean groups still keep it.

festivals.title: The birthday of Epicurus
festivals.creator: The 10th of Gamelion, in January or February
festivals.why: His will left money for an annual gathering on the day.

festivals.title: Panhellenic Symposium of Epicurean Philosophy
festivals.creator: February, at Pallini near Athens
festivals.why: A free weekend of talks held every year since 2011 in the district where his family came from.

places.title: The Kerameikos
places.creator: Athens, Greece
places.why: The ancient cemetery by the Dipylon gate. The Garden lay somewhere just outside it on the road to the Academy. Nothing is marked, but you can walk the road.

places.title: Herculaneum and the Villa of the Papyri
places.creator: Ercolano, near Naples, Italy
places.why: The town buried in 79 CE. The villa that held the only library to survive from antiquity is partly excavated at its edge.

places.title: National Archaeological Museum
places.creator: Naples, Italy
places.why: The bronzes from the villa and some of the carbonised scrolls, most of them works by the Epicurean Philodemus.

places.title: The Getty Villa
places.creator: Pacific Palisades, California, United States
places.why: A full-size reconstruction of the Villa of the Papyri, with its long pool and gardens. Free with a timed ticket.

places.title: Samos
places.creator: North Aegean, Greece
places.why: The island where Epicurus was born to Athenian settlers and grew up. Green, quiet and good for walking.

ethics.title: Prudence
ethics.text: The beginning and the greatest good. From it come all the other virtues, because it shows that one cannot live pleasantly without living well.
ethics.practice: Before one choice today, reckon its pleasures and pains a week out.

ethics.title: Friendship
ethics.text: Friends give security and joy, and the wise will sometimes suffer and even die for a friend. Friendship dances round the world, says one saying, calling us to wake to happiness.
ethics.practice: Do something for a friend today that they did not ask for.

ethics.title: Justice
ethics.text: A pact neither to harm nor be harmed. Injustice is bad because the fear of being found out never leaves.
ethics.practice: Is there anything you hope nobody finds out? Put it right.

ethics.title: Simplicity
ethics.text: Those who need luxury least enjoy it most. Plain living is a training in freedom.
ethics.practice: Go without one comfort today, and notice whether you are less happy.

ethics.title: Gratitude
ethics.text: The ungrateful forget past goods and are always starting to live. The wise are thankful and do not grow old in spirit.
ethics.practice: Thank one person for something from long ago.

ethics.title: Frankness
ethics.text: A friend tells you the truth about your faults, gently and in private, and takes it in return.
ethics.practice: Ask a friend what you most need to hear.

philosophy.title: Pleasure as the goal
philosophy.text: Every creature from birth seeks pleasure and avoids pain. That is nature’s guide. But the pleasure worth having is a body without pain and a mind without trouble.
philosophy.practice: Notice a moment today when nothing hurts and nothing is wanted. That is it.

philosophy.title: The limit of pleasure
philosophy.text: Once pain is removed, pleasure cannot be increased. It can only be varied. Chasing more past that point is a mistake about arithmetic.
philosophy.practice: Stop eating at the moment hunger ends.

philosophy.title: Death is nothing to us
philosophy.text: All good and evil lie in sensation, and death is the end of sensation. While we are, death is not. When death is, we are not.
philosophy.practice: Consider the time before you were born. Did it trouble you?

philosophy.title: The gods are no threat
philosophy.text: If there are gods they are perfectly blessed, and a blessed being has no anger and no favourites. Nature runs by itself.
philosophy.practice: Name one fear of punishment you carry that has no basis.

philosophy.title: Atoms and void
philosophy.text: The world is bodies moving in space. Souls are made of fine atoms and scatter at death. Nothing comes from nothing, and nothing vanishes into nothing.
philosophy.practice: Look at an object and think about what it was a thousand years ago.

philosophy.title: The swerve
philosophy.text: Atoms sometimes deviate without cause. So the future is not fixed, and our choices are our own.
philosophy.practice: Find one thing you assumed was fated and treat it as open.

philosophy.title: The three kinds of desire
philosophy.text: Natural and necessary, natural and unnecessary, and empty. Most unhappiness comes from taking the third kind for the first.
philosophy.practice: Reclassify one thing you think you need.

philosophy.title: Live unnoticed
philosophy.text: Public life brings rivalry, fear and dependence on the crowd. A small circle of friends in a garden is safer and sweeter.
philosophy.practice: Do one good thing today that nobody will ever know about.

intro: Epicurus was born in 341 BCE on the island of Samos, the son of an Athenian schoolmaster. He grew up in the unsettled years after the death of Alexander the Great, when the old city-states had lost their independence and ordinary people had little say in their own fate. He studied the atomism of Democritus, taught for some years on the coast of Asia Minor, and in 306 came to Athens with a group of friends and bought a house with a garden.

The community that lived there was unlike the other schools. It included women and slaves as full members. It took no part in politics. Its members studied, gardened, wrote to one another when apart and ate together, and its founder was loved in a way that struck outsiders as close to worship. Epicurus wrote some three hundred rolls. Three letters, two collections of sayings and some charred fragments survive.

His starting point is that pleasure is the good and pain the evil, as every infant and animal shows. This got him a reputation he did not deserve. The pleasure he meant is not the pleasure of banquets. It is the condition of a body that is not in pain and a mind that is not afraid, and it is easily reached. Hunger is cured by bread, thirst by water. What ruins human life is not lack of luxuries but two fears and one mistake: fear of the gods, fear of death, and the belief that we need things we do not need.

Against the fears he offered physics. The universe consists of atoms moving in empty space. Worlds form and dissolve by natural causes. The gods, if they exist, live in perfect peace and have nothing to do with us. The soul is made of atoms too and scatters when the body dies, so that death is simply the end of feeling and cannot be bad for the one who has died. Against the mistake he offered a sorting of desires into the necessary, the merely natural and the empty, with the advice to satisfy the first, enjoy the second and drop the third.
And he prized friendship above everything else that wisdom provides. A meal without a friend, he said, is the feeding of a lion or a wolf.

The school spread quickly. In Rome it produced Lucretius, whose poem On the Nature of Things is its fullest surviving statement. Christianity found its denial of providence and of an afterlife intolerable, and for a thousand years Epicurean meant glutton and atheist. The rediscovery of Lucretius in 1417, and later the scrolls dug out at Herculaneum, brought it back, and it fed into modern science and the modern idea that happiness in this life is a proper aim.
This Onda follows the Garden’s way: the four remedies in the morning, a sorting of desires, a plain meal with a friend, some study of nature, and a grateful look back at night.
guide.origin: Athens, in a house with a kitchen garden outside the Dipylon gate
guide.era: Epicurus founded the Garden in 306 BCE. Schools lasted across the Greek and Roman world for six centuries

figures.name: Epicurus
figures.bio: The founder. Frail for much of his life, generous to his friends, and by all accounts in his school the kindest of men. He freed several of his slaves in his will.

figures.name: Democritus
figures.bio: The earlier philosopher from whom Epicurus took atoms and void. Known as the laughing philosopher.

figures.name: Metrodorus of Lampsacus
figures.bio: His closest friend and the school’s second mind. He died first, and Epicurus provided for his children.

figures.name: Hermarchus of Mytilene
figures.bio: A companion from the early days and the first head of the Garden after the founder.

figures.name: Leontion
figures.bio: A member of the Garden and a former courtesan, who wrote a treatise against Theophrastus that Cicero grudgingly admired for its style.

figures.name: Themista of Lampsacus
figures.bio: A philosopher of the school to whom Epicurus addressed letters. Later writers named her as a model of a wise woman.

figures.name: Philodemus of Gadara
figures.bio: Epicurean teacher and poet on the Bay of Naples, friend of Virgil’s circle. Most of the Herculaneum scrolls are his works.

figures.name: Lucretius
figures.bio: Roman poet of whom almost nothing is known beyond his poem in six books.

figures.name: Diogenes of Oenoanda
figures.bio: A wealthy old man in a mountain town of Lycia who inscribed Epicurean philosophy on a wall for strangers and those not yet born.

figures.name: Pierre Gassendi
figures.bio: French priest and scientist who cleared Epicurus’s name and reconciled atomism with Christianity, opening the way for modern physics.

history.detail: His parents are Athenian colonists. He says he turned to philosophy at fourteen, when his teachers could not explain what came before chaos in Hesiod.
He does his military service in Athens in the year Alexander dies. The Athenians are then expelled from Samos, and he joins his family as a refugee at Colophon.
He begins teaching and gathers the friends who will stay with him for life.
He buys a house in the city and a garden outside the walls for eighty minae.
After two weeks of pain from a blocked bladder he gets into a warm bath, asks for wine, tells his friends to remember his teachings, and dies. His will frees four slaves.
On the Nature of Things appears in Rome. Cicero reads it and remarks on its genius.
The eruption buries a villa at Herculaneum with its philosophical library of perhaps a thousand scrolls.
Diogenes sets up his inscription. In the same century the emperor Marcus Aurelius funds a chair of Epicurean philosophy at Athens.
The schools fade. The emperor Julian is glad that most Epicurean books are already lost.
The papal secretary Poggio Bracciolini discovers a manuscript of the poem in a German monastery and has it copied.
His study of the life and philosophy presents Epicurus as sober and admirable.
Workmen tunnelling at Herculaneum find the carbonised scrolls. Reading them has taken until the present century, lately with X-ray imaging.
A collection of eighty-one Epicurean maxims is found in a fourteenth-century manuscript in the Vatican Library.

concepts.text: The beginning and end of the blessed life.
concepts.detail: It comes in two kinds. Moving pleasures are those of satisfying a want. Settled pleasure is the state of having no want and no pain, and it is the higher.
Reached by removing false beliefs about the gods, death and what we need. It is described as a calm, not as excitement.
God is not to be feared, death is not to be felt, the good is easy to obtain, the terrible is easy to endure.
Natural and necessary desires have a limit and must be met. Natural but unnecessary ones only vary pleasure. Empty ones have no limit and come from opinion.
Everything is made of indivisible particles differing in shape and size, falling through infinite void. There are countless worlds.
Without it atoms would fall in parallel for ever and never meet. With it there is collision, a world, and freedom from strict fate.
The soul is a body of fine atoms spread through the flesh. It cannot feel or think apart from the body, and it disperses like smoke at death.
Lucretius: look back at the eternity before we were born. It was nothing to us. Nature holds it up as a mirror of the time to come.
There is no justice in itself. It is a compact made for mutual advantage, and what is just can differ between places and times.

facts.text: Above the gate of the Garden, according to Seneca, was written: stranger, here you will do well to stay; here our highest good is pleasure.
Seneca, a Stoic, quotes Epicurus with approval in letter after letter, saying that what is true is his own.
A common Epicurean epitaph across the Roman empire read: I was not, I was, I am not, I do not care.
The word for an unbeliever in rabbinic Hebrew, apikoros, comes from his name.
Karl Marx wrote his doctoral thesis on the difference between the atomism of Democritus and that of Epicurus.
Scrolls from Herculaneum that could never be unrolled began to be read in 2023 using scans and machine learning.

sensitivity.note: Epicurus is easy to mistake for a preacher of indulgence. His school taught the reverse: plain food, few wants, and friendship. This Onda keeps to what the surviving texts say and marks later tradition as such.
requiredCaveats: Epicurus advised withdrawal from public life. Critics from Cicero onward have asked who then looks after the city.
The arguments against fearing death are meant for the thought of one’s own death. They are not offered as a comfort for grief, which Epicurus himself felt and honoured.
